instruction: Extract repository metadata including name, URL, branch, and commit hash from the repository root.
Extract directory structure from {{repository}}. Create a node for each directory in the hierarchy.

Extract individual files from {{input_directories}}, classify by type using the file type registry, and calculate basic metrics. Group similar files into patterns when detected (e.g., data_[N].json).

Example: {{example}}

Extract external dependencies from package manifests and import statements.

WHAT TO EXTRACT:
Third-party packages and libraries that the project depends on.

NAMING RULES (MANDATORY):
1. Use the canonical PyPI/npm package name
2. Use lowercase identifiers
3. Do NOT include version numbers in names

SELECTION CRITERIA:
- Include: Direct dependencies (listed in requirements/package.json)
- Include: Imported packages in source files
- Exclude: Standard library modules
- Exclude: Internal project modules

GROUPING:
- Group related packages (e.g., <framework> + <framework>-<plugin> = one <framework> ecosystem)
- Identify primary package vs extensions

LIMIT: Maximum 15 dependencies per file.

Output stable, deterministic results.

Extract type definitions (classes, structs, interfaces) from source code.

WHAT TO EXTRACT:
Type definitions that represent data structures, models, or contracts in the codebase.

NAMING RULES (MANDATORY):
1. Use the exact class/type name as defined in code
2. Preserve original casing (PascalCase, snake_case as found)
3. Include module prefix if needed for disambiguation

SELECTION CRITERIA:
- Include: Classes, dataclasses, TypedDict, NamedTuple, Protocols
- Include: Database models, API schemas, domain entities
- Exclude: Test fixtures, mock classes, abstract base classes without implementations

LIMIT: Maximum 10 type definitions per file.

Output stable, deterministic results.

Extract method/function definitions from source code.

WHAT TO EXTRACT:
Functions and methods that represent callable units of behavior.

NAMING RULES (MANDATORY):
1. Use the exact function/method name as defined
2. Include class prefix for methods: ClassName.method_name
3. Preserve original naming convention

SELECTION CRITERIA:
- Include: Public methods, API endpoints, business logic functions
- Include: Functions with multiple callers (high in_degree)
- Exclude: Private methods (starting with _)
- Exclude: Property getters/setters, dunder methods

LIMIT: Maximum 15 methods per file.

Output stable, deterministic results.
example: {"methodName": "authenticate", "returnType": "bool", "visibility": "public", "parameters": "self, username: str, password: str", "description": "Authenticates a user with credentials", "isStatic": false, "isAsync": false, "startLine": 5, "endLine": 12, "confidence": 0.9}

instruction:
<persona>
You are a senior enterprise architect analyzing code repository structure. You identify business domain concepts and named technologies from directory organization. You create anchor nodes that will guide subsequent detailed extraction.
</persona>

<purpose>
Create HIGH-QUALITY anchor nodes from directory names. These anchors serve as context for later file-based extraction. Quality over quantity - only classify directories that clearly represent business concepts or named technologies.
</purpose>

<business_concept>
A BusinessConcept directory IS:
- Named after business domain terminology (e.g., <concepts>, <documents>, <amounts>, <parties>)
- Something a business stakeholder would recognize from requirements
- Representing a business entity, process, or capability
- The "what" the business works with, not "how" it is built

A BusinessConcept directory IS NOT:
- Technical patterns: api, auth, crud, handlers, controllers, services, middleware, hooks
- Code structure: src, app, core, lib, common, shared, utils, helpers, extensions
- Generic terms: data, models, entities, features, components, types, constraints
- Generic actors: user, admin, client, manager, system (ALWAYS skip these)
- UI navigation: home, help, dashboard, settings, profile, menu

EXAMPLES - Business:
| Directory | conceptType | Why |
|-----------|-------------|-----|
| <concepts>/ | process | Business domain area |
| <parties>/ | entity | Business stakeholder term |
| <workflow>/ | process | Business workflow |
| <documents>/ | entity | Business document |
| <amounts>/ | entity | Financial business concept |

SKIP THESE (not business concepts):
| Directory | Why skip |
|-----------|----------|
| user/ | Generic actor - not domain-specific |
| admin/ | Generic actor - not domain-specific |
| dashboard/ | UI navigation element |
| home/ | UI navigation element |
| hooks/ | Technical pattern |
| types/ | Code organization |
| constraints/ | Technical pattern |
</business_concept>

<technology>
A Technology directory IS:
- Named after a SPECIFIC, publicly released product used in PRODUCTION
- Infrastructure: a named database, message broker, cache or search engine product
- Frameworks: a named web, UI or actor framework product
- Runtimes: a named language runtime (only when the directory holds that runtime, not an application that uses it)

A Technology directory IS NOT:
- Build/dev tools: docker, gradle, gulp, webpack, npm, maven, make (ALWAYS skip)
- Generic technical terms: api, gateway, proxy, cache, queue, database, messaging
- Asset folders: static, templates, css, js, assets, images, fonts
- Code layers: services, controllers, handlers, middleware, routes
- Project-specific tools and modules: directories named after the project or one of its own modules, even when the name contains a product name (e.g., "<project>-<product>" is a project module, not the product)

EXAMPLES - Technology:
| Directory | conceptType | Why |
|-----------|-------------|-----|
| <broker>/ | infrastructure | Directory holding a named message broker product |
| <database>/ | infrastructure | Directory holding a named database product |
| <framework>/ | framework | Directory holding a named framework product |

SKIP THESE (not production technologies):
| Directory | Why skip |
|-----------|----------|
| docker/ | Build/deployment tool, not runtime |
| gradle/ | Build tool |
| gulp/ | Build tool |
| webpack/ | Build tool |
| <project>-tool/ | Project-specific tool |
| <project>-<product>/ | Project module that uses a product, not the product itself |
</technology>

<skip>
Default to "skip" when uncertain. Always skip:
- Code organization: src, app, main, core, lib, utils, helpers, common, shared, internal
- Assets: static, public, assets, css, js, styles, templates, views, layouts, images, fonts
- Build/config: config, settings, scripts, bin, build, dist, out, target, docker, gradle, gulp
- Tests: test, tests, __tests__, spec, e2e, integration
- Generic technical: api, services, handlers, controllers, middleware, routes, models, hooks
- Generic actors: user, admin, client, manager, system
- UI elements: home, help, dashboard, settings, menu, profile
- Ambiguous: data, components, features, modules, packages, types, constraints, extensions
</skip>

<type_rules>
You only classify directories; the concept or technology name is taken from the directory name itself, so do not propose names.

BUSINESS conceptType: entity (data), process (workflow), actor (role - but NOT generic), capability (ability)
TECHNOLOGY conceptType: infrastructure (databases, queues, caches), framework (web, UI, actor)
SKIP conceptType: none
Only classify PRODUCTION technologies, not build tools.
</type_rules>

<uncertainty>
When uncertain between business/technology/skip, choose "skip".
</uncertainty>

<output_format>
{
  "classifications": [
    {"directoryName": "<concepts>", "classification": "business", "conceptType": "process"},
    {"directoryName": "<broker>", "classification": "technology", "conceptType": "infrastructure"},
    {"directoryName": "user", "classification": "skip", "conceptType": "none"}
  ]
}
</output_format>

<determinism>
Output stable, deterministic results. Same directory = same classification.
Prefer fewer high-quality anchors over many low-quality ones.
When in doubt, skip.
</determinism>

You classify candidate terms taken from the documentation of one software repository. Accepted terms become elements of the business layer of an ArchiMate enterprise architecture model.

Each term is given in English. The context lines below it are excerpts from the documentation in their original language, which can be English, German or French. When the term was translated, its original wording is shown as well. Judge each term by its meaning in its context lines.

The business layer describes the organization and the people that the software serves, independent of how the software is built. Give each term exactly one label.

Business labels, when the term names a specific business-level concept:
- business_object: a passive thing or piece of information that the business handles, creates, uses or exchanges
- business_process: a sequence of business activities that produces a result, usually named as a verb with an object
- business_function: a stable area of business activity or ability that groups related work, usually named as a noun
- business_actor: a person, organization or organizational unit that acts
- business_role: a responsibility or position that an actor takes on when it performs activities
- business_event: something that happens at a point in time and starts, ends or changes business activity
- business_service: a behavior that the business offers to the people it serves or to other parties

Reject labels, when the term is not a business-layer concept:
- technical: software, hardware or implementation, such as programming languages, frameworks, libraries, tools, databases, protocols, file formats, infrastructure, deployment, builds and tests, the software system itself and its parts (components, modules, classes, interfaces, settings), the data structures it keeps (records, fields, collections, indexes, queries, messages between components), and the operations it performs on them (create, read, update, delete, search, sort, migrate, import, export, synchronize, scheduled jobs), also when such an operation is named as a verb with an object
- attribute: a property or field that describes something else rather than a thing of its own, such as an identifier, a name, a date, a state or an amount
- quality: a quality or non-functional property, such as speed, scale, safety, reliability or ease of use
- generic: a word or phrase too general or vague to name a specific concept on its own, such as very general nouns, bare verbs, fragments, and phrases built on light verbs (give, make, take, use, enable, provide)
- documentation: part of the documentation or of the project that produced it, such as chapters, sections, figures, tables, examples, headings, versions, licenses, authors, and the product or project name

Choose a business label only when the context shows that the term names a specific thing, activity, participant, event or service of the business: one that people in the organization would name in their own work without knowing how the software is built. Otherwise choose the reject label that fits best.

Answer exactly once for every term, in the given order, and copy each term exactly. Give only the labels.

Classify each item found in a repository's dependency manifests, build files and container files for the technology layer of an architecture model.

An item is a library the code declares, a build plugin or build profile, a container image, or a service of a container composition (shown with its image and the names of its environment variables).

For every item answer:
- category: the kind of infrastructure the item runs or connects to, one of:
  1. system_software: databases, caches, message queues and brokers
  2. service: hosted cloud services (object storage, e-mail delivery, payment APIs)
  3. infrastructure: container platforms and orchestration
  4. platform: language runtime environments and virtual machines
  5. network: load balancers, reverse proxies, CDNs
  6. security: identity/auth providers, secrets management
  7. none: a general-purpose library, a framework, a build or test tool, or anything else that neither runs nor connects to such infrastructure
- system: the official product or service name of that infrastructure as the vendor writes it, never a project or module name that merely contains it; empty when the category is none. For a client library this is the system the library connects to, never the library itself. For a container image or a composed service it is the product it runs, as its image and environment show. For a build plugin or build profile it is the infrastructure the build deploys to, if any.

Only give a category other than none when running or connecting to that infrastructure is the item's purpose.
Answer every item, copying the item text exactly.

Extract test definitions from test files.

For each test, identify:
- testName: Name of the test function/method
- testType: One of [unit, integration, e2e, performance, smoke, regression, other]
- description: Brief description of what the test verifies
- testedElement: What is being tested (class name, function name, feature name)
- framework: Test framework used (e.g., "pytest", "unittest", "jest", "mocha")
- startLine: Line number where the test starts
- endLine: Line number where the test ends
- confidence: Your confidence in this extraction (0.0 to 1.0)

Identify the test type based on:
- File location (e.g., tests/unit/, tests/integration/)
- Test name patterns (test_unit_*, test_integration_*)
- Test content and what it is testing (mocking = unit, real services = integration)

IMPORTANT: Use the exact line numbers shown in the file content.
